title: Neighbors
hook: the literal ones: know their names
tomorrow: what does faith at work sound like when nobody mentions God?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two proverbs that turned out to describe one friend, the loving one and the honest one: at all times. Today, the people we didn't pick at all. They just live nearby.
screen: `AT ALL TIMES.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO JUST LIVE NEARBY.`

segments.voice: Doorbell cameras make it easy to watch a whole street and know nobody on it. The package thief gets a nickname; the woman two doors down never gets a name at all. And Christians read the word neighbor two ways. Is your neighbor everyone on earth, or the person next door? Both readings come from the Bible, and they pull in different directions.
screen: `WATCH THE STREET, KNOW NOBODY.` → `EVERYONE, OR NEXT DOOR?` → `TWO READINGS, BOTH BIBLICAL.`

segments.voice: Leviticus gives the command: “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” A lawyer asks Jesus the obvious follow-up: “And who is my neighbour?” Jesus answers with a Samaritan, from a people John says Jews had little to do with, who stops on the road for a wounded stranger. Then Jesus turns the question around: “Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?” The lawyer answers: “He that shewed mercy on him.” The first view takes that and runs: neighbor has no border. Anyone in need, anywhere, of any people. Its best case: a love that stops at the edge of your own group isn't the love Jesus described. The second view doesn't deny any of that; it guards the near. Proverbs: “better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.” Its best case: a love for all humanity that never learns one name on its own street can stay an idea. And here's what's worth telling a friend: the Samaritan's mercy happens on one road, to the one person in front of him. The widest story in the Gospels is also a very local one. Some Christians start with the world, some with the street. Both start with a face.
screen: `WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?` · `VIEW ONE: NO BORDER.` · `VIEW TWO: GUARD THE NEAR.` · `ONE ROAD, ONE FACE.` · then, large: `THE LITERAL NEIGHBOR.`

segments.voice: Listen for the sounds of the people around you: a door, a car, a voice through a wall, a dog down the block. Each one belongs to someone with a name. If you pray, hold the nearest one before God; if not, just wonder who they are.
Neighbors. Anyone in need, Jesus says; the person near, says Proverbs. Today, the literal ones, starting with a name.
Your line: the literal neighbor. Love for everyone still needs one name on your own street. Day seventeen-eighteen, done.

howItsDone: Christians read 'neighbor' both widely, as anyone in need, after the Good Samaritan, and locally, as the people next door; some churches organize street meals, welcome visits for new neighbors, or simple efforts to learn names.

chat.says: pop knows every name on our street. i don't know ONE. but isn't everyone my neighbor anyway?
options: Both. Jesus widens neighbor to anyone in need, and Proverbs keeps the one next door. Learn one name.
Yes. Everyone on earth is your neighbor, so the people on your street aren't special.
No. Your neighbor is the person next door; people far away aren't really your concern.
chat.meaning: The Samaritan story opens neighbor to anyone in need; Proverbs says better a neighbor near than a brother far off. The wide reading doesn't cancel the literal one.

Leviticus.meaning: a book of the Torah, full of laws for holy living

Samaritan.meaning: someone from Samaria, a people living near Judea

Proverbs.meaning: a Bible book of short sayings about wise living
